name: Facial thread lift (cheek lifting)
lead: A facial thread lift is a minimally invasive procedure in which thin threads, some barbed or coned, are placed under the skin to raise sagging facial tissue without cutting away skin. For the cheeks, it is used to lift the midface, restore cheek position and soften the nasolabial fold, giving a higher, fuller-looking cheekbone area and a more defined midface.[1][3]

People choose it as a shorter-recovery alternative to a surgical facelift. Surgical rhytidectomy remains the reference procedure for lifting facial tissue and removing excess skin, with costs quoted in the thousands of dollars,[4] while thread lifts are described as a simpler option involving small entry points.[3] Some threads are coated with hyaluronic acid, and some practitioners pair them with energy devices such as microfocused ultrasound.[1][2]

Published material on thread lifts consists mainly of registered trials and case reports of complications. A registered trial compared hyaluronic acid-coated and non-coated threads for midface lifting, and another combined threads with microfocused ultrasound; results are not available.[1][2] Case reports describe rare complications including a pseudolymphoma, a nerve injury and an artery pseudoaneurysm.[6][7]
infobox: Threads (varied; some barbed, coned or hyaluronic acid-coated)

paras: Thread lifting inserts threads into the subcutaneous layer so that they hold or reposition tissue; the technique is described as simplifying the lifting that a facelift achieves surgically.[3] Threads vary in material and design, and in recent years hyaluronic acid-coated versions have been tested for midface work.[1]
A case report notes that thread lift is also done for jowls and describes it as a blind procedure in which key structures are not directly visualised.[7]

Wikipedia describes thread lifts using silicone threads with barbs that pull facial and neck skin upward without removing skin, and mentions anti-ptosis (APTOS) sutures as one approach; it says combining threads with other methods is said to give better results.[3] Threads differ in material, absorbability and barb or cone design, and there is no single standard type.

A surgical facelift (rhytidectomy) lifts deeper facial layers and redrapes skin, and it was the third most popular aesthetic surgery in 2019 according to American Society for Aesthetic Plastic Surgery figures cited by Wikipedia.[4] Thread lifting is positioned as a less invasive alternative with a shorter recovery period.[3]

Wikipedia traces the facelift from early-1900s skin-pulling procedures through the SMAS technique introduced after Tord Skoog’s subfacial approach in the late 1960s and 1970s, deep-plane and subperiosteal methods in the 1980s, and a focus since the 1990s on restoring volume and lifting upward rather than backward.[4] It describes mini-facelifts and skin-only lifts as involving less downtime, notes recovery of 2 to 3 weeks for a MACS lift versus 3 to 4 for a traditional facelift, and says a skin-only lift can last 5 to 10 years while mini-lifts are more temporary.[4] Hematoma is the most common facelift complication, followed by nerve injury, and smoking raises the risk of skin necrosis.[4] Prices cited for 2008 ranged from about US$2,500 in India and Panama to about US$15,000 in the US and Canada.[4]

In appearance terms, the cheek region carries much of what people read as youthful or sculpted: fullness over the cheekbone, a smooth transition to the lower eyelid, and a shallow nasolabial fold. Thread lifting for the cheeks aims at those features by elevating tissue upward, and the registered midface trial lists nasolabial fold correction alongside lifting as its target.[1]
Wikipedia notes that facelift surgery shifted from the 1990s toward restoring volume and lifting upward rather than backward, a goal that midface thread lifts echo.[4]

Wikipedia states that combining threads with other rejuvenation methods is said to give better results.[3] One registered trial pairs threads with microfocused ultrasound, and another compares hyaluronic acid-coated threads with uncoated ones.[1][2] Mini-facelifts and skin-only lifts are described as surgical middle options with less downtime than a full facelift.[4] A 2012 case report of complications from APTOS sutures, cited on Wikipedia, describes correction with a MACS lift and fat grafting.[3]

Wikipedia reports that physician Vincent Wong has called it among the most dangerous procedures an aesthetic practitioner can perform, noting that some threads stay in the tissue and cannot be pulled out, and that a 2021 BBC investigation of training courses recorded poor infection control and severe patient pain.[3] The article also notes UK aesthetic practitioners needed no mandatory qualifications.[3]

Case reports describe cutaneous pseudolymphoma after a thread lift,[6] glossopharyngeal nerve compression causing hypertension after a jowl-region lift,[7] and a superficial temporal artery pseudoaneurysm two months after a thread lift.[5] Authors of the nerve case note that widespread use has increased the variety and frequency of complications.[7] The pseudolymphoma report lists small bruises, mild redness, transient altered sensation and mild swelling as the comparatively low-incidence usual complications.[6]

In the BBC investigation of 2021, as described on Wikipedia, 26 cosmetic training academies in Liverpool offered courses costing 150 to 5,000 pounds and lasting from a few hours online to a few days in person. An undercover nurse reported poor infection control, blood vessels punctured during training and a patient in severe pain, and Ashton Collins of Save Face said complications were likely if course graduates went on to perform treatments.[3]

The BBC Three documentary Under the Skin: The Botched Beauty Business, presented by Ashni Lakhani and released on 24 June 2021, reported that an undercover nurse saw the tutor touch objects and then the patient's face, and saw the procedure done on a chair rather than a bed.[3] Wikipedia describes the silicone barbed threads it covers as non-absorbable, which is one reason removal is described as difficult.[3] Practitioners and regulators in different countries set different training requirements, so qualification of the person performing the lift varies.[3]

Thread lifts are marketed under labels such as non-surgical facelift and APTOS lift, as an option between injectables and surgery.[3] Facelift remains among the most popular aesthetic surgeries; ASAPS figures cited by Wikipedia place it third in 2019.[4] Costs quoted on Wikipedia for surgical facelifts range from about US$2,500 to US$15,000 depending on country, in 2008 figures; no price for thread lifts is given there.[4]

A completed 144-participant registered study (NCT07916103, started 2024) compared HA-coated and non-HA threads for midface lifting and nasolabial fold correction.[1] A 45-participant registration (NCT04157218, started 2019, status unknown) examined thread lifting with microfocused ultrasound.[2] No published results are available. Published literature otherwise consists of complication case reports.[6][7]

timeline.event: Eugen Holländer reportedly performs an early facelift in Berlin.[4]
Tord Skoog develops subfacial dissection, published in 1974, leading to the SMAS facelift technique.[4]
Mitz and Peyronie describe the SMAS.[4]
Start of the volumetric period in facelift surgery, emphasising volume and upward lift.[4]
Case report by Sapountzis et al. on treating complications of APTOS thread lifts.[3]
Facelift is the third most popular aesthetic surgery by ASAPS figures; thread-lift trial NCT04157218 begins in November.[2][4]
BBC Three investigation of thread-lift training courses airs on 24 June.[3]
Trial of HA-coated and non-HA threads for midface lifting begins.[1]

lore.intro: Thread lifts are discussed as a lunchtime or non-surgical alternative to a facelift, with debate about how long results last and how safe the procedure is in less-trained hands.[3]

claims.claim: A thread lift gives a facelift-like cheek lift without surgery.
claims.believers: Providers and patients describe lifted cheeks, a softer nasolabial fold and short recovery through small entry points.[3]
claims.experts: Wikipedia describes thread lifts as a less invasive alternative; registered trials of midface lifting have not published results.[1][3]

claims.claim: Combining threads with other treatments improves results.
claims.believers: Practitioners pair threads with energy devices or other rejuvenation methods.[2][3]
claims.experts: A registered trial pairs threads with microfocused ultrasound; no published results are available.[2]

claims.claim: Thread lifts can go wrong in untrained hands.
claims.believers: Physician Vincent Wong has called it among the most dangerous procedures an aesthetic practitioner can perform.[3]
claims.experts: Case reports describe pseudolymphoma, nerve injury and artery pseudoaneurysm, and the BBC investigation recorded poor infection control.[3][5][6][7]

card.summary: Threads placed under the skin to hoist the cheeks; minimally invasive, with unclear efficacy data and reported complications.
card.note: Practitioner training and complications have drawn media scrutiny.

quick.overview:
A thread lift uses threads inserted under the skin to lift the cheeks and midface without cutting away skin.
Trials are registered, but published outcome data are not available.
quick.mechanism: Threads, some barbed or coated, anchor and elevate tissue, and are placed through small entry points.
quick.risks: Physician and media reports describe infection, vessel puncture and pain, and some threads cannot easily be removed. Practitioner qualifications vary by country.

chain: Threads are placed under the skin through small entry points
Barbs or cones hold and reposition sagging tissue
Cheeks sit higher and the nasolabial fold looks softer
angle.text: A thread lift is used to raise drooping cheek and midface tissue without removing skin, giving a higher-looking cheekbone area and a more defined midface. People choose it as a shorter-recovery option than a surgical facelift.
